In the account where Peter heals a man paralyzed from birth, "his feet and ankles became strong" (Acts 3:7): the ankles, previously unable to bear weight, suddenly regain the strength and stability needed to walk.
G4974.origine: The Greek word σφυρόν comes from a root expressing the idea of firmness and structure. It specifically designates the joint where the bones and ligaments connecting the leg and foot come together, the area where the body supports itself to stand and move.
G4974.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 3:7, where Peter heals a man born lame. The detail of the strengthened ankle emphasizes that the healing is not a spectacle, but a complete and functional restoration of the body — the miracle touches even the joints, that is, the places that truly allow walking. It is a very concrete, anatomical word that supports the physical reality of the miracle.
G4974.portee: This healing of the ankles reminds us that Jesus and His apostles healed people in a holistic and visible manner. The anatomical detail shows that the miracle was not an illusion or psychological suggestion, but a real transformation of the body. For the Christian, this affirms that God's power extends to every part of us, even the most humble.

sens: By a small margin, not quite reaching the whole
With a very great proximity, an overwhelming majority
G4975.detail:
1. This word expresses a near-totality: something approaches so close to completeness that it differs only by a tiny part. In Acts 13:44, "almost the whole city" means that the entire city or nearly so gathered to hear Paul — a human gathering that expresses extraordinary interest. Similarly, in Hebrews 9:22, "almost all" that pertains to the law is purified by blood: the text acknowledges a few rare exceptions but establishes a nearly absolute rule, this being fundamental in the system of sacrifices.
2. The word emphasizes a proportion so great that it borders on universality. Acts 19:26 reports that Paul "almost" convinced all of Asia: not every person without exception, but an audience so massive and an impact so profound that the movement spread throughout the territory, in a nearly universal way. This nuance acknowledges a reality on the threshold of totality, just below it.
G4975.origine: The word comes from the root ἔχω (to have, to hold), and its basic image evokes spatial proximity or approach: it is what happens very close to you. In common Greek, σχεδόν primarily denotes proximity of place, then by extension any approach to a state or limit — here, the approach to totality. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses this word in similar contexts, always to express a near-reaching of a limit.
G4975.emploi: The New Testament uses σχεδόν three times, exclusively in Acts and the Epistle to the Hebrews, in narrative or doctrinal contexts where the extent of a phenomenon must be emphasized as nearly total. In Acts, it describes the influx of a crowd (13:44) and the spread of an influence (19:26): in both cases, it is to show the power of the Gospel and its massive impact. In Hebrews 9:22, the word establishes a theological rule: purification by blood is not an exception, it is the nearly universal law of the ancient sacrificial system. The meaning remains constant: what touches on totality without completely reaching it.
G4975.portee: This word invites the reader to grasp the scope and effectiveness of God's work: not only does Paul preach, but entire crowds rush to him; not only do a few sacrifices purify, but almost everything that defiles requires blood. "Almost" does not diminish the strength of the testimony — on the contrary, it makes it more credible and striking by acknowledging that we approach a truth that exceeds our expectations. It is the irresistible impact of divine grace.

sens: The outward appearance of a thing, its visible form
The look, the way something presents itself or behaves
The transient and changing order of the present world
G4976.detail:
1. The "figure" is the external aspect that one sees of a thing or a person — what stands out. It is the shape and silhouette, what is first shown.
2. This word also refers to the way something functions or manifests — how it presents itself to us. Philippians 2:8 shows Jesus in the "figure of a man," meaning he presented himself as a man to everyone.
3. Paul uses "figure of the world" to describe the visible, changing, and transient order of the current world — not what is permanent, but what passes and constantly changes. In 1 Corinthians 7:31, "the figure of this world passes" means that all this visible and temporal system disappears, while what comes from God remains.
G4976.origine: The word σχῆμα comes from the verb ἔχω (to have, to hold) and literally denotes what is "held" or "formed" — what has taken a visible shape. It is related to the root μορφή (form), but σχῆμα emphasizes the changeable external appearance, while μορφή indicates the deep and stable form or nature of a thing. In Hebrew, this term often translates פֹּת (pôth), which also denotes appearance and distinction of someone.
G4976.emploi: The word appears clearly only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 7:31, Paul urges believers not to cling to the world by using it "as not using it," for the "figure of this world passes" — that is, everything that is visible, temporary, and changing. In Philippians 2:8, he qualifies Jesus as in the "figure of a man" to show how he presented himself externally to everyone — not as a dazzling deity, but under the appearance of an ordinary man. The word thus denotes the fleeting external aspect, as opposed to what is eternal or essential.
G4976.portee: For the Christian, this distinction between the "figure" of the world (temporary, changing) and the permanent reality invites us not to cling to it as if it were definitive. We are not called to abandon the world, but to use it without being trapped in it: this transforms our relationship to material goods, fashions, and the conventions of the moment. It is an invitation to live in inner detachment while being present here and now.

sens: To split or tear a surface, fabric, or object by separating it forcefully
To make a rupture, a brutal separation
To divide into opposing groups, to be disunited
G4977.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to tear or split something in two. This is what happens to the temple veil at the moment of Jesus' death (Matthew 27:51, Mark 15:38, Luke 23:45): this great curtain that closed the sanctuary is torn from top to bottom, a gesture of God that opens access to the Holy of Holies. In the parable of the garment (Luke 5:36), one does not tear a new fabric to patch an old garment, for that would ruin the new. It is also tearing Jesus' garments by sharing them (John 19:24), or the nets under the weight of the fish (John 21:11).
2. The word evokes an opening, a separation that occurs. When the heavens open at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:10), the Greek verb schizô describes this heavenly tearing: the visible world parts to reveal the Spirit descending.
3. In a figurative sense, the word describes a division, a rupture of unity. When the assembly in Jerusalem divides over the issue of resurrection (Acts 23:7) or when in Iconium the population splits between those who support the apostles and those who oppose them (Acts 14:4), the text says it "tears apart" — it splits into opposing and irreconcilable factions.
G4977.origine: The Greek verb schizô comes from a root that evokes the action of splitting or dividing. In ancient Greek, it often translates the Hebrew bâqua', which also means to split or burst. The word family includes schisma (schism, division, or rupture), which denotes a permanent fracture within a group. The basic image is that of a violent, irrevocable separation.
G4977.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, and Luke use it to describe the tearing of the temple veil — a pivotal event of the Passion. Luke also uses it in a parable about the garment. John places it in two contexts: the sharing of Jesus' crucified garments, and the miraculous rupture of the nets under the abundance of fish. In Acts, Paul uses the word in a figurative sense: the division of an assembly or crowd. The verb can thus denote a real physical separation, a supernatural opening, or a social and spiritual fracture.
G4977.portee: This word reminds us that Christ came to accomplish a radical break with the old covenant: the veil that separated sinners from the Holy of Holies is torn, opening access to God. It also shows how the Gospel divides people — not out of malice, but because some receive it and others reject it. The division that Jesus causes is not an end in itself, but the inevitable consequence of his presence and his word.

sens: Tear, rupture of a fabric
Disagreement, dissension within a group
Doctrinal or ecclesiastical schism
G4978.detail:
1. Tear, rupture of a fabric: a physical rupture in a cloth. In Matthew 9:16 and Mark 2:21, Jesus speaks of a piece of new cloth sewn onto an old garment: this "tear" would be worse, for the new fabric would pull away and enlarge the hole. This is the most concrete image of the word.

2. Disagreement, dissension within a group: a rupture of unity among people. In John 7:43 and 10:19, there was "division" among the crowd because of Jesus — some recognized him, others did not. This is the sense of rupture applied to the harmony of the group.

3. Doctrinal or ecclesiastical schism: a serious separation within the Christian assembly over issues of faith and practice. In 1 Corinthians 1:10, Paul urges the Christians in Corinth not to have "divisions": he targets the factions that form around different spiritual leaders (Paul, Apollos, Cephas). This rupture wounds the Church in its very body.
G4978.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb schizo, which means "to split, to tear." Σχίσμα is the result of this action: the split, the rupture produced. The root evokes the image of a blade that parts, that separates in two. The word is first used for a material rupture, then for any rupture of unity — social, doctrinal, spiritual.
G4978.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and John. In Matthew and Mark (2 occurrences), it refers to a tear in fabric in the literal sense. In John (3 occurrences: 7:43, 9:16, 10:19), it refers to a division among the Jews regarding Jesus: the crowds split in two, torn by opposing opinions. In 1 Corinthians (3 occurrences: 1:10, 11:18, 12:25), Paul addresses the Church divided by factions and quarrels: he denounces these "divisions" as a serious wound to the body of Christ. In Paul, the word takes on a strong spiritual and moral charge: it is not only a rupture, but a betrayal of the unity that the Spirit creates.
G4978.portee: This word reveals to the Christian faith two things. First, the unity of the Church is not a mere aspiration: it is a gift from Christ and the Spirit, which should never be torn by factions and doctrinal quarrels. Secondly, each "division" is an evil that wounds the Christian testimony: John shows that disputes about Jesus divide even the crowd; Paul asserts that factions in Corinth contradict the nature of the Church, a single body with one Spirit.

sens: braided or coiled link made of fibers or reeds, used to tie or hold something
figuratively: a bond that binds or restrains
G4979.detail: 1. The word concretely refers to a rope, that is, a braided or coiled link used to tie, hold, or operate something. In John 2:15, Jesus makes a whip with ropes to drive out the merchants from the temple — these are flexible and supple links. In Acts 27:32, the soldiers cut the ropes of the lifeboat to abandon it: the ropes are what held the vessel. 2. Figuratively (less attested here but inherent to the word), the rope symbolizes a binding link or what restrains someone, such as a moral or spiritual hindrance.
G4979.origine: The Greek word σχοινίον is a diminutive of σχοῖνος, which originally meant reed or rush — the fibrous plant from which ropes were made. This origin in plant material reminds us that ancient ropes were often made from fibers of aquatic plants. The diminutive suffix indicates a rope of modest dimensions or quality.
G4979.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament according to available sources. First in John 2:15, where it is used to describe the ropes of an improvised whip — a tool for correction. Then in Acts 27:32, where it refers to the ropes that hold a lifeboat, a purely practical maritime object. In both cases, it refers to concrete and material objects, without particular theological weight: it is the technical, simple, and effective word for naming a braided link.
G4979.portee: This small word reminds us of two acts of rupture or separation in the New Testament: that of Christ driving out the profaners from the temple, and that of the sailors abandoning the lifeboat. It helps us visualize the stark reality of these scenes and grasp how concrete actions — cutting a rope, wielding a whip — embody choices and breaks. For the reader, it is a word that anchors the biblical narrative in the materiality of daily life.

G4980.fr: to be vacant or to dedicate oneself
sens: (of a place) to be empty, unoccupied
(of a person) to be free, to have available time
(of a person) to dedicate oneself entirely to something, to devote oneself
G4980.detail:
1. When a building or house is vacant, there is no one inside — it is empty. The house of the demon, after being cast out, is found "empty, swept, and adorned" (Matthew 12:44), perfectly unoccupied and well arranged.

2. To be free or available means to have time ahead, not being occupied by other obligations. When one has time, one can give it to what truly matters.

3. To dedicate oneself to something means to put all one's strength into it, to devote oneself completely. Paul tells spouses to "give themselves to prayer" (1 Corinthians 7:5): for a set time, they abstain from one another precisely to dedicate themselves entirely to prayer, free from any other concern.
G4980.origine: The word comes from the Greek scholè, which denotes leisure, free time dedicated to study or reflection. Scholazô thus literally means "to have leisure," "to be at leisure." The word has retained this image: to be free, to have one's time, or (for a thing) to be unoccupied. This root gives the French word "école" (where one once had the leisure to learn) and "scholastic."
G4980.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. First in Matthew 12:44 and Luke 11:25, where it describes a house as "empty" — the concrete sense of an unoccupied place, without inhabitants. Then in 1 Corinthians 7:5, where Paul uses it figuratively: spouses can "give themselves to prayer," meaning to free themselves from the rest to dedicate themselves entirely to what is spiritual. The word thus plays on the image of availability: a place without occupant, or a person without occupation, free for another task.
G4980.portee: This word reminds us that time is a precious commodity. It first teaches us that the absence of God leaves a void: a soul unoccupied by good runs the risk of being filled with evil. It also teaches us that sometimes we must voluntarily free ourselves from our legitimate occupations — marriage, business — to dedicate ourselves to spiritual matters. It is a call to discernment of time and priorities.

sens: Place where teaching and learning occur
Group of disciples gathered around a master
Set of doctrines or methods common to several people
G4981.detail:
1. School primarily refers to the building or room where teaching takes place: it is a physical space provided for the master to speak and the disciples to listen. In Ephesus, Paul enters daily into the school of Tyrannus to teach about the way of the Lord (Acts 19:9), transforming this place of pagan rhetoric into a platform to proclaim the Gospel.
2. By extension, school refers to the group of people who gather to learn together from a master. It is no longer just the room, but the community that forms there — the disciples are united by their desire to learn and follow the one who teaches them.
3. Figuratively, school can also evoke the entire set of ideas, methods, or principles that a master or tradition transmits to its followers: a "school of thought." It is the intellectual and spiritual heritage that disciples receive and perpetuate.
G4981.origine: The Greek word scholē comes from a root that first means "leisure" or "free time" — for to learn or discuss, one must free oneself from ordinary occupations. Gradually, in ancient Greece, the word changed meaning: it first designated debate or dispute (what one does during leisure to exercise one's mind), then the place where this occurs, and finally the group of thinkers who gather around a common doctrine. This evolution reflects the history of philosophical schools, from Plato to Aristotle.
G4981.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:9. Paul, after proclaiming Christ in the synagogue of Ephesus for three months, faces criticism from some unbelievers who deny the way of the Lord. He then separates from these opponents and gathers the disciples around him, teaching daily in the school of Tyrannus. This passage shows how a school — a place of classical Greek teaching — becomes the setting for Christian evangelization: Paul transforms the work of rhetoric and debate into the proclamation of the Kingdom of God. The use of the word also reflects Paul's missionary strategy, who uses existing social structures to spread the Christian message.
G4981.portee: This word reminds us that Christian teaching is transmitted in ordinary life, in spaces where people naturally gather. The school of Tyrannus was not a basilica or a temple, but a place of civic training that Paul invested with his message. This encourages the believer to recognize that faith is not limited to religious places: it is spoken and learned wherever one is willing to listen. It is also an image of the nascent Church that gradually forms outside official structures, through the living transmission of doctrine and a community of disciples.

sens: Deliver from danger, death, or destruction
Heal from an illness
Save life, preserve it
Save from sin and spiritual condemnation
Obtain salvation, be saved (passive or reflexive sense)
Accomplish the salvation of someone
G4982.detail:
1. Saving someone from danger means pulling them from peril, from an immediate threat. This is the most concrete sense: delivering from a storm (Matthew 8:25: "Lord, save us"), from imminent death. The image is that of physical rescue.
2. Healing an illness means restoring health: the woman who had been sick for twelve years is "healed" by touching Jesus' garment (Mark 5:28), the blind man who regains his sight is "saved" from his blindness (Mark 10:52).
3. Saving life means preserving it — whoever wants to "save" their life by refusing the path of discipleship will lose it; whoever loses it for the Gospel will save it (Matthew 16:25).
4. The spiritual sense: saving from sin and divine condemnation. Jesus will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); John 12:47: Jesus comes not to judge the world, but to save it — to rescue it from spiritual destruction.
5. Being saved (passive or reflexive form): receiving salvation. Romans 10:13: "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved"; Acts 2:47: "the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved".
6. Accomplishing salvation, realizing the act of saving: the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost (Luke 19:10); he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
G4982.origine: The verb σῴζω comes from a root that evokes the idea of "making whole" or "preserving integrity." It is related to the noun σῶς ("whole," "entire") and the noun σωτηρία ("salvation"). In classical Greek, it primarily denotes physical rescue. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew yasha (יְשַׁע), which means "to deliver" or "to save" in a broad sense — from danger, from the enemy, and progressively from sin. This lineage shows how the word carries within it the idea of complete restoration: returning the saved person to integrity, life, health, and righteousness.
G4982.emploi: The word σῴζω appears more than a hundred times in the New Testament, far more than any other term. It is used by all four Gospels to describe Jesus' healing miracles (Mark 5:34: "your faith has saved you"), his acts of deliverance from danger (Matthew 8:25), and especially to state his central mission: to save the lost (Luke 19:10). In Paul and the epistles, the word acquires a theological predominance: it denotes salvation in Christ in the face of divine judgment and sin. Paul specifies its three temporal dimensions: salvation as the past work of Christ (Romans 8:24: "we have been saved"), as current grace (Acts 2:47: "those who were being saved"), and as future fulfillment (Hebrews 9:28: Christ will save "those who are waiting for him"). The verb is constructed with ἀπό ("from") or ἐκ ("out of") to specify what one is saved from: from their sins, from wrath, from death.
G4982.portee: This word is at the heart of the Christian faith: it summarizes God's plan for humanity. Understanding "save" helps the believer grasp that Jesus did not come to condemn or judge, but to rescue from sin and death. The word also invites one to distinguish the three times of salvation — past (what was accomplished at the cross), present (the grace received each day), and future (the promised glory). For the reader, it is a word of comfort: just as Jesus saved the sick and sinners of his time, he still invites anyone to call on his name to be saved.

sens: The physical body of a person, living or dead
The body of an animal
An object or material substance
The concrete reality, as opposed to the shadow or representation
The assembly of believers united to Christ as one body
A person, an individual
G4983.detail:
1. The human physical body, in all its materiality: either living, with its members and sensations ("If your right eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out," Matthew 5:29), or dead, as when Jesus' body was taken down from the cross (Matthew 27:58-59). The body is the place where the soul and spirit dwell, the instrument by which we live and act in the world.

2. The bodies of animals, living or dead: a less frequent usage, but it shows that the word designates any corporeal being, from the horse in James 3:3 to the sacrificial animals in the temple.

3. Material, inanimate objects: 1 Corinthians 15:37-38 speaks of the grain you sow, the body that grows — it is a lifeless body, a solid form.

4. The substantial reality as opposed to its shadow or representation: Colossians 2:17 opposes the body (the reality) to the shadow. It is like saying that the true body of Christ is himself, while the Old Testament was only its shadow.

5. The entire Church, considered as one living body of which Christ is the head: "we are members of his body" (Ephesians 5:30). Each believer is a member, and all together form the body of Christ, an organic unity animated by the same Spirit.

6. An individualized person, a human being counted as a unit: this sense appears especially in Revelation 18:13, where "body" refers to the slaves sold in the market — here the word shifts from the physical sense to the sense of person.
G4983.origine: The Greek word σῶμα (sôma) comes from an Indo-European root that evokes the idea of standing upright, having a form. It translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew words בָּשָׂר (flesh) and גְּוִיָּה (corpse or carcass), showing that the Greek body and the Hebrew body are not identical: the Hebrew emphasizes the fragility of flesh, while the Greek highlights the visible and defined form. The family of the word includes compounds that enrich this notion of bodily unity.
G4983.emploi: The word σῶμα appears 120 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Gospels. It primarily denotes the concrete human body: in Matthew and Mark, the dead body of Jesus at the Passion; in Luke, the living body with its needs (food, clothing); in John 2:21, the temple meaning the resurrected body of Jesus. In Paul, the word gains a moral and theological significance: the body is subject to sin (Romans 6:6, 7:24), but also the place where the Spirit dwells (1 Corinthians 6:19) and the instrument of a living offering to God (Romans 12:1). Finally, Paul develops the image of the body of Christ: the entire Church is the body of Christ, of which believers are the members (1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4). This image transforms the meaning of the word: from physical, it becomes communal and spiritual.
G4983.portee: Understanding that the body is not a prison of the soul to be despised, but a gift from God, an instrument of service and communion. For the Christian, it is an invitation to honor their body through purity and self-control (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), and also to recognize that they are part of the body of Christ, the Church — which means they are never alone, always connected to other believers in an organic unity, and responsible towards them.

sens: Belonging to the body, concerning the physical body
Having a material, tangible form
G4984.detail:
1. The word designates what belongs to the body or concerns it directly. In 1 Timothy 4:8, Paul speaks of bodily exercise, meaning the physical training of the body, in contrast to the spiritual exercise of godliness.
2. The word can also qualify what has a material and visible form, which can be perceived by the senses. Luke 3:22 shows this: the Holy Spirit descended on Jesus "in bodily form," meaning that His presence was manifested in a concrete and visible way, like a dove, and not purely spiritual or invisible.
G4984.origine: The word comes from the root σῶμα (sôma), which means "body" in Greek. This term designates the physical body as a whole, in contrast to the soul or spirit. The adjective σωματικός naturally derives from it to express everything that is "of the body" or "related to the body." It is therefore a classic compound word: it indicates belonging or relation to the carnal, visible, and material reality.
G4984.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament according to known testimonies. Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 4:8 to qualify the exercise of the body — physical training — which he considers useful but less than spiritual godliness. Luke uses it in 3:22 to describe the manifestation of the Holy Spirit in bodily form to Jesus at His baptism. In both cases, the word marks the distinction between the visible and material on one hand, and the spiritual or immaterial on the other. Its usage always emphasizes that it concerns something that touches or relates to the body and matter.
G4984.portee: This word helps the reader understand that the body is not inherently bad — it can be exercised and disciplined — but it does not have ultimate value. Spiritual formation, godliness towards God, surpasses mere physical preparation. At the same time, Luke reminds us that God does not disdain the material world: He revealed Himself in a bodily, visible, recognizable way to His Son and to those who looked upon Him. This is a biblical balance: the body matters, but the spirit matters more.

sens: In a physical manner, in the body or by the body
In a real and concrete way, not merely in figure or appearance
G4985.detail:
1. The word describes what is done or manifested physically, tangibly, by the body or in the body. In Colossians 2:9, Paul asserts that "the fullness of the deity dwells bodily" in Christ: not merely in idea or promise, but in a real and incarnate manner, in the historical person of the Son of God.

2. The adverb also emphasizes the concrete and true nature of the divine presence, in contrast to what would be merely symbolic or spiritual in appearance. The deity does not merely "dwell" from afar in Christ; it establishes itself there truly, visibly, in all its fullness.
G4985.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective meaning "of the body" (soma), itself related to the idea of physical body, of tangible reality. The suffix -ōs in adverb transforms the adjective into manner or mode. This root is also found in "somatic" in modern French.
G4985.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:9. Paul uses it to refute a heresy that diminished the divinity of Christ by reducing it to an appearance or a distant emanation. By saying that the deity dwells "bodily" in Jesus, he affirms the real incarnation of the living God: Christ is not an immaterial or illusory intermediary, but the true God present in a concrete human body.
G4985.portee: This word reminds the believer that God has not hidden Himself in mysterious abstractions, but has made Himself visible and tangible in Jesus Christ. It is an invitation to confident faith: the God we seek is not a distant idea, but a person we can meet, know, and follow.

sens: Christian disciple from Berea who accompanied the apostle Paul
G4986.detail: Sopater is a man from Berea in Macedonia, son of Pyrrhus. He is part of the group of disciples who escorted Paul on his journey to Jerusalem, likely to bring the relief offering collected from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 20:4).
G4986.origine: The name Sopater is composed of two Greek elements: "so" (σώ) meaning "safe" or "whole," and "pater" (πατήρ) meaning "father." The full name thus evokes the idea of a "whole" or "salutary" father. It is a common Greek name in the Mediterranean world of the first century.
G4986.emploi: Sopater appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:4, where he is presented as one of Paul's traveling companions. He represents one of the many Christians of the apostolic age who devoted themselves to the service of the Church and to accompanying the apostles in their missions.
G4986.portee: The mention of Sopater reminds us that the early Church was alive and active in the cities of Macedonia. It also shows that Paul surrounded himself with faithful disciples, trustworthy men, to support him in his apostolic ministry and travels in the service of the Gospel.

sens: To pile up, accumulate in a heap
To load, overload to the point of being crushed under the weight
G4987.detail:
1. The word describes the action of amassing, piling something up in a heap or accumulation. It is the concrete image of weight that gradually adds up. In Romans 12:20, "to heap burning coals on the head of your enemy" means to accumulate upon him the weight of acts of kindness — a striking image of divine judgment or guilt that increases.
2. Figuratively, the word also designates being overwhelmed, crushed by an accumulation of weight. In 2 Timothy 3:6, the expression "silly" literally translates as "loaded with sins" — these women are figuratively burdened, weighed down by the ever-increasing burden of their faults, until they lose their discernment.
G4987.origine: The word comes from the Greek σῶρος (sôros), which means "heap," "pile." It is a verb formed to express the action of accumulating, of creating a heap. The basic image is very concrete: it is that of materials piled up on each other, gaining in weight and volume.
G4987.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 12:20, Paul cites the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) to speak of covering his enemy with burning coals — an ancient biblical metaphor meaning that by showing kindness to one who hates us, we heap upon him evidence of his own guilt or confront him with his own hardness. In 2 Timothy 3:6, Paul describes women "loaded with sins" (literally "amassed with sins"), burdened by an accumulation of sinful habits that make them vulnerable to deception.
G4987.portee: This word teaches that sin accumulates and weighs down the one who commits it, until it paralyzes them morally and spiritually. It also shows that our acts of kindness, even towards an enemy, have real weight — they add up and pile up in judgment. It is an invitation to take seriously the progression of evil as well as that of good.

sens: Leader of the Jewish synagogue in Corinth
Companion and brother in Christ of the Apostle Paul
G4988.detail:
1. Sosthenes was the leader of the Jewish synagogue in Corinth, responsible for the order and religious life of this community. During Paul's trial before the proconsul Gallio, the angry crowd seized him and beat him in front of the tribunal, while the magistrate remained indifferent to what was happening (Acts 18:17).
2. The same Sosthenes, transformed by faith in Christ, became a companion of Paul and is mentioned as a co-signer of Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, where Paul refers to him as "brother Sosthenes" (1 Corinthians 1:1), revealing a deep spiritual brotherhood.
G4988.origine: The Greek name Sosthenes literally means "he who saves strength" or "strong and savior," composed of σῴζω (to save) and σθένος (strength, power). It is a Greek name that reflects values of strength and rescue. The Bible does not tell us how this character bore this name, but the story of his transition from persecutor to persecuted, then to beloved brother, gives a poignant irony to this patronymic.
G4988.emploi: Sosthenes appears twice in the New Testament, probably as the same person at two stages of his life. First, he is the leader of the synagogue in Corinth who opposes Paul during his first missionary visit around 50-52 A.D. (Acts 18:17). Then, a few years later, he appears as a companion of Paul during the writing of the first epistle to the Corinthians, written from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 1:1). This remarkable transformation—from beaten persecutor to brother in Christ—illustrates how the gospel touched even Paul's adversaries and integrated them into the Christian community.
G4988.portee: The story of Sosthenes teaches the transformative power of the Gospel: a religious leader who opposed Paul, who even suffered violence because of his hostility to the Christian message, becomes a brother and collaborator in proclaiming this Gospel. It shows that no position is too high, no opposition too firm, for God's grace to reach and renew a life. It is a call to hope for the conversion even of those who seem farthest from faith.

sens: Companion of the Apostle Paul
Relative of Paul mentioned in the final greetings
G4989.detail: Sosipater is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Paul's letter to the Romans. He appears among those sending their greetings to the Romans alongside Timothy, Lucius, and Jason (Romans 16:21). Paul refers to him as "my fellow worker," indicating that he actively collaborated with Paul in his ministry. The term "relatives" used by Paul to refer to Sosipater, Lucius, and Jason suggests that they may have been his close associates or fellow Jews.
G4989.origine: The name Sosipater is a Greek compound formed from "sôs" (safe, saved) and "patēr" (father), which would literally mean "he whose father is saved." It is a Greek name borne by a disciple of Paul, indicating that the Apostle's collaborators came from diverse backgrounds, some having Greek names, others Hebrew or Latin names.
G4989.emploi: Sosipater appears only once in Scripture, in Romans 16:21, where Paul greets the Christians in Rome by mentioning his collaborators. He is presented as a "fellow worker" of Paul, meaning he participated in the missionary work and preaching of the Gospel. The fact that Paul mentions him among the first in this list of greetings suggests his importance in the apostolic ministry, although the Bible does not provide further details about his history or specific activities. His name does not appear anywhere else in the New Testament.
G4989.portee: Sosipater represents those faithful collaborators whose work has remained discreet but essential to the development of the apostolic ministry. His example reminds us that many servants of God work in the shadows, without human recognition, but with the certainty that their work alongside the apostles bears lasting fruit for the Gospel.

sens: one who rescues someone from danger or death
one who liberates from oppression or domination
one who preserves, keeps alive
one who brings salvation, redemption
God who saves His people
Jesus Christ, the savior sent by God
G4990.detail:
1. The savior is primarily one who rescues from death or peril: the word comes from the verb "to save" and literally designates one who pulls someone from destruction (Acts 5:31).
2. It is also one who liberates from slavery or domination—a political role that the title commonly bore in antiquity, granted to kings and great leaders (Acts 13:23: God raised up a Savior from the lineage of David for Israel).
3. The savior preserves, maintains, keeps alive those he protects (Philippians 3:20: our Savior will come from heaven).
4. In the language of biblical faith, the savior brings spiritual salvation, deliverance from sin and eternal death (2 Timothy 1:10).
5. God alone is the Savior of the Old Testament people—He who delivered them from Egypt and protects them (1 Timothy 1:1).
6. Jesus Christ is proclaimed the Savior of the world: the one whom God sent to redeem humanity (John 4:42, Titus 1:4: "Jesus Christ our Savior").
G4990.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb sōzō (σώζω), "to save." It translates in Greek the Old Testament Hebrew verbs such as yāsha' (יָשַׁע), "to deliver, to save." The image is that of someone pulling another from danger or death. In Ptolemaic Egypt and during the Roman period, it was a title given to kings and great generals, recognized as those who preserve their people. The Christian Bible adopts this honorable title for God first, then for Christ.
G4990.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline and Petrine epistles. For God: He is called "our Savior" or "God our Savior" because of His work of deliverance (Luke 1:47, 1 Timothy 2:3, Titus 1:3). For Jesus Christ: He is named "Savior" as the one in whom the promise of salvation is fulfilled, often with specifications—"Savior of the world" (John 4:42), "Savior of the body, that is, the Church" (Ephesians 5:23). The title emphasizes that Jesus continues God's work: He saves, liberates, preserves. In the later epistles (1 and 2 Peter, 2 Timothy, Titus), the title "Jesus Christ our Savior" becomes almost a formula of confession (Titus 2:13, 2 Peter 1:1).
G4990.portee: This title imbues the figure of Christ with authority and tenderness: He is not merely a master of wisdom, but the one who rescues us from nothingness, sin, and death. It signifies that salvation is not a human conquest, but a gift from the One who has the power to save. For the believer, recognizing Jesus as Savior means entrusting Him with one's entire life, knowing oneself to be rescued from destruction and assured of forgiveness. It also reveals that the Christian faith does not rest on our efforts, but on divine initiative: God loved us enough to send us a Savior.

sens: Deliverance from immediate danger, preservation from death
Healing or physical restoration
Fulfillment of God's promises for His people
Reconciliation with God and forgiveness of sins through Christ
Current state of the saved believer assured in God
Final and eternal fulfillment of God's plan
G4991.detail:
1. Deliverance from danger: the word primarily describes a concrete help in the face of peril. Noah is saved from the flood (Hebrews 11:7), the Israelites are delivered from Pharaoh, and Paul escapes shipwreck (Acts 27:34).
2. Healing or restoration: more broadly, it encompasses everything that preserves life and health. The context can be physical or spiritual.
3. Messianic promises: the Bible speaks of a "Savior" (Luke 1:69) and a "word of salvation" (Acts 13:26) that God sends to His people — Jesus Himself is this salvation.
4. Reconciliation through Christ: salvation primarily means the end of the rupture with God, the forgiveness of sins, access to the Father through Jesus (John 4:22, Acts 4:12). It is the unique work of Christ: "There is no salvation in any other" (Acts 4:12).
5. Present possession: the believer already possesses salvation — he is justified, forgiven, at peace with God. It is a reality that one "obtains" right now (1 Peter 1:9, Philippians 1:19).
6. Future completion: salvation will be fully realized at Christ's return, when believers will be freed from all suffering and the presence of evil (Romans 13:11, Hebrews 9:28).
G4991.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "sōz-" (to save, to preserve). In Hebrew, it translates several terms — יְשׁוּעָה (yesha'a, help) and תְּשׁוּעָה (teshout), all stemming from the idea of widening, giving space, delivering from narrowness or threat. This racial image persists: the one who saves "widens" the life of the one in peril. That is why God is called the "Savior" of His people.
G4991.emploi: This word is very frequent in the New Testament (48 occurrences), especially in Paul and the author of Hebrews. In the Gospels, it primarily denotes the awaited messianic salvation — God's envoy to deliver Israel (Luke 1:69, 1:71, John 4:22). After Pentecost, the term becomes central: it is through Jesus alone that one obtains salvation (Acts 4:12, Acts 13:26). Paul emphasizes that this salvation is offered to both Gentiles and Jews (Romans 11:11, Acts 28:28). Gradually, the focus shifts from the future to the present: the believer possesses salvation now and experiences its effects (Philippians 1:19, 2 Corinthians 1:6), but it will be fulfilled when Christ returns (Romans 13:11, 1 Peter 1:5). The word can also refer to the "message" or the "Gospel" of salvation (Acts 13:26, Ephesians 1:13).
G4991.portee: For the believer, this word encapsulates the essence of faith: God loved us and sent Jesus to save us — to reconcile us with Him, to forgive us, to give us a place with Him. It is both a foundational act (we are forgiven), a present possession (we enjoy peace with God), and a hope (everything will be fully restored). This salvation is not reserved for anyone — it is offered to all who believe, without exception. It is the heart of the Gospel.

sens: The act of saving, the fact of being saved from death or peril
Deliverance brought by God to the people of Israel, fulfillment of His promises
That which saves, that by which one obtains salvation
Eternal salvation, deliverance from sin and condemnation by the grace of God
G4992.detail:
1. Salvation is primarily the act of saving someone from death or danger — the concrete idea of the word. In Luke 2:30, when Simeon says, "my eyes have seen your salvation," he refers to baby Jesus Himself as the one who brings salvation to His people.
2. In the Old Testament, "salvation" refers to God's intervention to deliver Israel from its enemies or trials, the fulfillment of His promises of protection and restoration.
3. Salvation is also that which saves concretely: the grace of God (in Titus 2:11, "the grace of God, source of salvation, has been manifested"), the armor of salvation (in Ephesians 6:17, the helmet of salvation protects the spiritual soldier).
4. In the New Testament, salvation fully takes on its spiritual meaning: it is the deliverance from sin and eternal condemnation by the grace of God in Jesus Christ, offered to all peoples (Acts 28:28, "this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles").
G4992.origine: The word comes from the root "soter" (savior, the one who saves). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates words like "yeshoua" (deliverance) and "shalom" (peace, wholeness). These words initially described concrete salvation — escaping an enemy, being healed, surviving — before enriching the spiritual meaning of deliverance from sin that the New Testament fully reveals in Jesus Christ.
G4992.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in this sense (Luke 2:30), but it is at the heart of the evangelical message. Simeon, a righteous and devout man, recognizes in the child Jesus the salvation awaited for generations — God's salvation offered to all peoples (Luke 3:6 and Acts 28:28). The adjective "salutary" is found in the New Testament to qualify God's grace (Titus 2:11) and spiritual armor (Ephesians 6:17), showing that salvation is both a present reality and a constant protection for the believer.
G4992.portee: Recognizing Jesus as God's "salvation" means understanding that our deliverance from sin and death comes through Him alone. For the Christian, salvation is not an abstract concept: it is the concrete and free action of God that saves, protects, and restores us. This truth invites gratitude and trust: our entire life depends on the salvation that God offers us in Jesus Christ.

sens: to have a clear and lucid mind, to return to reason
to master one's thoughts and desires, to be moderate
not to overestimate oneself, to remain humble in one's judgments
G4993.detail:
1. To have a clear and lucid mind, to return to reason — It is primarily to regain mental clarity after disturbance or alienation. The man possessed in Mark 5:15 "was sitting, clothed, and in his right mind": after Jesus delivered him, he regains his clear thought, balance, and dignity. The word opposes confusion, loss of control, and madness.
2. To master one's thoughts and desires, to be moderate — It is the ability to remain measured in one's behavior and emotions. In Titus 2:6, young men are to be "sober-minded," meaning temperate, without excess. In 1 Peter 4:7, "be sober and watchful": one must cultivate this sobriety of soul that allows living with discernment, far from drunkenness or excess.
3. Not to overestimate oneself, to remain humble in one's judgments — It is to refuse vanity and pride. Romans 12:3 asks each one to "not think of himself more highly than he ought to think," to "put on modest thoughts": to have sound mind is to assess one's strengths accurately, without arrogance.
G4993.origine: The word comes from the adjective σώφρων (sōphron), which means "wise, prudent, sound-minded." It is composed of σῶς (sōs, "healthy, intact") and φρήν (phrēn, "mind, heart"), literally meaning "having a healthy mind." It is a classical Greek ideal: lucidity and self-control. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates Hebrew roots related to discernment and wisdom.
G4993.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and Peter. Mark and Luke use it to describe the healed possessed man (Mark 5:15, Luke 8:35): Jesus has brought this man back to reason. Paul uses it to speak of true wisdom: to have sound mind is not to think oneself superior to others (Romans 12:3), it is to remain balanced in one's piety (2 Corinthians 5:13). In Titus and Peter, it is about exhorting to self-control and sobriety, essential virtues for any Christian who wants to live a faithful and prayerful life. Everywhere, it is the opposite of folly, excess, and pride.
G4993.portee: This word invites the Christian to seek mental clarity and self-control, in opposition to any form of recklessness or debauchery. It reminds us that faith is not a spiritual drunkenness or uncontrolled exaltation, but a lucid and orderly adherence to God. It is also a call to humility: to rightly estimate one's own worth is to know oneself as one truly is, neither less nor more. For the one who follows Jesus, it is to live with discernment and sobriety.

sens: Teach someone to have good sense and self-control
Shape someone's character through education
Bring someone back to healthy and balanced thoughts
G4994.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to give someone good sense — that is, practical wisdom, judgment, the ability to govern oneself well. It involves a formation of the heart and mind, not just the transmission of knowledge. In Titus 2:4, Paul speaks of "learning" young women to love their husbands and children in a healthy way — it is about training them in regulated and reasonable affections.
2. The word also evokes the idea of bringing someone back to their senses, as one would do with someone who has lost their mind or is going off track. It is about calling to order, correcting a misguided behavior by restoring inner balance.
3. By extension, it is about cultivating temperance, restraint, and self-control — these virtues that prevent a person from being carried away by their passions or impulses.
G4994.origine: The verb comes from the adjective σώφρων (sôphrôn, "sensible, wise, temperate"), formed from the root meaning "sound mind" — literally "one who has their senses well in hand." The family of this word encompasses the idea of sôphrosunê, temperance, this fundamental moral virtue among the Greeks. It is a term deeply marked by Greek philosophy, but which the authors of the New Testament adopt to speak of Christian virtues.
G4994.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:4. Paul uses it when describing the educational mission of older women: they must "learn" young women to love their husbands and children. The context shows that it is not merely an intellectual transmission, but a formation of the emotional and moral heart. It is an act of education and mentoring aimed at restoring or cultivating practical wisdom in the most intimate relationships. The choice of this rare verb emphasizes the importance of this intergenerational transmission.
G4994.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that spiritual education is not limited to intellect: it involves the formation of the heart and character. Authentic Christian life requires practical wisdom, self-control, and emotional balance — especially in family ties. It is a call to transmit not theories, but a living virtue: knowing how to love with discernment, restraint, and balance is a grace that is taught and learned.

sens: Self-control, control of one's thoughts and actions
Ability to act with discernment and prudence
Gift of the Holy Spirit that preserves from disorder and fear
G4995.detail:
1. Wisdom here primarily means self-control, the ability to govern oneself and direct one's thoughts, emotions, and actions with order and restraint. It is a spirit that is not dominated by passions or fear. In 2 Timothy 1:7, Paul asserts that this spirit of self-control comes from God himself, not from timidity or disarray.

2. This term also evokes practical discernment: knowing how to act wisely, with prudence and intelligence, in the circumstances of life. It is the opposite of impulsivity or mental confusion. A Christian who possesses this wisdom does not panic in the face of difficulties but reflects and chooses their actions according to God's will.

3. In the context of 2 Timothy, this wisdom is presented as a divine gift, alongside strength and love: it is the Holy Spirit who communicates it to the believer so that they are not paralyzed by fear, but act with confidence and good sense.
G4995.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to admonish," "to correct," or "to bring back to reason" — the idea of a spirit being set back on the right path. It is close to the Greek word for "wise" or "sensible" (sophron), which designates one who has a sound and balanced mind. The root suggests the image of a mind restored, preserved from folly or disorder.
G4995.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:7. Paul uses it to characterize the gift that God has granted to Christians facing trials and persecutions. Here, wisdom does not refer to theoretical knowledge or erudition, but to a disposition of the heart and mind: the ability to remain clear-headed, self-controlled, and confident in God even under pressure. It is an antidote to the timidity and fear that could paralyze the witness of Christ.
G4995.portee: For today's Christian, this word reminds us that self-control is not primarily a fruit of human will or austere self-discipline, but a gift of the Holy Spirit. It invites us to ask God for this spirit of strength, clarity, and good sense, especially when fear threatens to paralyze us. It is a word of encouragement: the disciple of Christ does not receive a spirit of confusion, but of discernment and self-control to live and witness with courage.

sens: With self-control, restraint, and discernment
In a balanced and reasonable manner, without excess
With prudence and good sense in practical life
G4996.detail:
1. Soberly means to act with self-control and restraint — to know how to control oneself, maintaining the balance of one's mind in the face of temptations and desires. In Titus 2:12, the Apostle Paul exhorts to live "soberly": to reject worldly desires and govern oneself by wisdom, righteousness, and godliness. It is the opposite of impulsivity or surrendering to passions.
2. It also means to act in a balanced and reasonable manner, without falling into excess. The word evokes someone who has their full consciousness, who thinks before acting, who refuses extremes. It is the mark of a healthy mind and a firm will to do good.
3. Practically, living soberly means making wise choices in daily life: in managing one's time, money, relationships, and pleasures. The context of Titus shows that this is an essential trait of a disciple of Jesus in "the present age."
G4996.origine: The Greek word σωφρόνως (sōphronōs) comes from the root σωφρονέω (sophronéō), which literally means "to have a sound mind." It is composed of σῶς (sōs, "whole, sound") and φρήν (phrēn, "mind, heart, understanding"). This image of a sound and integral thought dates back to ancient Greece, where prudence (sophrosunē) was considered a capital virtue. The word expresses the idea of maintaining one's mental and moral balance.
G4996.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:12. Paul uses it to describe how believers should live "in the present age." This context shows that sobriety does not mean bleak austerity or rigorism, but rather a clarity and self-control that enable the Christian to turn away from the traps of the world ("ungodliness and worldly desires") and to cling to true values: "wisdom, righteousness, and godliness." It is a practical and demanding virtue.
G4996.portee: For today's Christian, this exhortation to live soberly is profoundly relevant. It invites clarity in the face of the world's seductions (consumerism, endless entertainment, immediate gratifications) and to cultivate a self-control that brings freedom. Living soberly means deliberately choosing what truly matters: communion with God, justice, love for others. It also recognizes that this self-control is not a personal performance, but a fruit of God's grace.

sens: Balance and clarity of mind, common sense
Self-control, sobriety
Restraint in appearance and conduct
G4997.detail:
1. Modesty is primarily a mental health, a clarity of mind: it opposes madness or delirium. When Paul defends his integrity before Governor Festus, he asserts that he is not mad but speaking "words of truth and common sense" (Acts 26:25). It is the opposite of mental confusion.
2. It then refers to self-control, the mastery of one's impulses and desires. It is an inner sobriety, a restraint that governs behavior.
3. Finally, it is expressed in external appearance and demeanor: posture, clothing, gestures. Paul urges women to dress "with modesty and self-control" (1 Timothy 2:9), without luxury or ostentatious adornments, and to persevere "with modesty" in faith (1 Timothy 2:15).
G4997.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "to preserve" or "to keep healthy." It is composed of elements that evoke a sound mind, preserved from disturbance. It is a term widely used in Greek philosophy to describe the virtue of practical wisdom and self-control. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates concepts of moral order and wisdom.
G4997.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament: twice in Paul's letters to Timothy, and once in Acts. In Acts 26:25, Paul uses it to assert his mental health in the face of the accusation of being possessed by madness. In 1 Timothy 2:9 and 2:15, it characterizes the attitude that believing women should adopt: a modest restraint in appearance and a balanced perseverance in the life of faith. The meaning thus shifts from the mental plane (common sense) to the moral plane (self-control) and then to the behavioral plane (external restraint).
G4997.portee: Biblical modesty is not timidity or shame, but a mental clarity and self-control that reflect Christian sobriety. It invites the believer not to be dominated by desires, to ensure coherence between thoughts and actions, and to carry within oneself a peaceful and balanced presence. It is a concrete expression of the mastery that the Spirit brings.

sens: Who has a sound and judicious mind, who thinks clearly
Who masters their passions and appetites, who shows restraint
Who is sober, who does not abuse drink
Who lives with measure and balance in all areas
G4998.detail:
1. It is primarily a quality of one who reasons rightly, without folly or deviation: a moderate person is sound of mind, capable of discernment (1 Timothy 3:2 describes the overseer as being sober and moderate, thus able to judge wisely in the life of the church).

2. It also means self-control: mastering one's desires, emotions, and carnal appetites. It is restraint regarding excess (Titus 2:5 invites women to be moderate, a term close to the same vocabulary, and Titus 1:8 requires that the overseer be moderate, that is, self-controlled).

3. Concretely, it also means not drinking excessively, remaining sober: the absence of drunkenness is a visible and important sign in communal life.

4. In its entirety, it is living with measure and balance: neither deficiency nor excess, a harmony in conduct. Titus 2:2 lists this moderation among the marks of Christian maturity for older men.
G4998.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to save" or "to preserve" — with the idea of a soul safeguarded, protected by itself, not giving in to its impulses. It is found in words of the same family that evoke prudence and wisdom. It is a virtue highly valued in Greek philosophy, but the Bible makes it a requirement of Christian life.
G4998.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, all in the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy and Titus) — the letters where Paul structures the life of the church. It first describes qualities required for leaders: the overseer must be moderate (1 Timothy 3:2), as must the elder (Titus 1:8). It then extends to ordinary Christians: older men must cultivate it (Titus 2:2), and young women as well (Titus 2:5, where the text uses a term from the same family). It is a call to maturity and balance for the entire assembly of believers.
G4998.portee: This virtue reminds the Christian that they are not enslaved to their desires, but capable of governing themselves by grace. It is particularly required of those who lead the community — pastors, elders — because the people of God need balanced and self-controlled guides. It is also an invitation to wisdom: this moderation protects the life of the church and the Christian testimony.

sens: road station on the Appian Way, near Rome
G4999.detail: 1. Three Taverns (literally "Three Inns") is a roadside relay located on the famous Appian Way, one of the major roads leading to Rome. It was a place where travelers stopped to rest and eat (Acts 28:15).
G4999.origine: The name "tavern" comes from the Latin taberna, which designates a small shop or inn. The place owes its name to the presence of three inns that were located there, making it a well-known landmark for travelers on the road to Rome.
G4999.emploi: Three Taverns appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 28:15, at the end of Paul's journey to Rome. It is there that Christians from Rome come to meet Paul and his companions, showing the interest and concern of the church in Rome for the apostle. This place marks the final stop before arriving in Rome.
